hypothesis.title: The Invisible Coordinate
hypothesis.question: When a musical surface is held constant, can listeners still distinguish changes made only in the leftover degrees of freedom allowed by a constraint system?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If chord labels, tempo, phrase length, and arrangement form are held constant while only voicing habits, graph traversal habits, or phase/spectral microstructure vary, then listeners will distinguish versions above chance because those hidden coordinates carry stylistic and textural information not captured by the explicit surface.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: Basso continuo realizations show that individual performers can be identified from pitch-content features inside a historically constrained practice, so style can survive as a residue of choices left open by rules [S3]. Tonnetz-style combinatorial geometries define adjacency and available harmonic resources without determining the exact traversal or realization, leaving path behavior as a compositional variable [S5]. Audio watermarking via STFT phase bins and adjacent-bin log-magnitude differences shows that frequency-domain microstructure can carry robust information while remaining perceptually subtle, which makes it a plausible hidden coordinate for timbral identity [S6]. The electronic-production source supports the practical arrangement side: call and response, silence, and timbral layering can keep the overt form stable while expressive identity moves through texture and negative space [S1]. The ice source adds a process model: path and rate can select nearby metastable states rather than globally optimal ones, suggesting a harmonic protocol based on nearest accessible states rather than direct resolution [S4]. The quantum-generation source frames the same issue abstractly: premature readout collapses structured possibility, so composition should decide which layer remains coherent before commitment [S2].

recipe.title: Same Surface, Hidden Coordinate
recipe.bodyMd: Create a 60-second A/B/C study in which the obvious musical surface stays fixed while one hidden coordinate changes. Use an eight-chord Tonnetz-like path as the harmonic surface [S5]. Arrange it as two-bar call and two-bar response phrases, preserving the same rhythm, tempo, and section layout across all versions [S1]. Version A varies only griff-like realization habits: voicing density, register, doublings, and chord grips, motivated by basso continuo style identification [S3]. Version B varies only path behavior: shortest-path motion, delayed resolution, and one nearest-accessible metastable detour inspired by path-dependent phase formation [S4]. Version C keeps MIDI and levels fixed while applying subtle phase/spectral treatment such as seeded high-partial micro-delay or adjacent-bin EQ ripple, motivated by phase-domain watermarking [S6]. The disconfirming result is clear: if blind listening cannot identify which coordinate changed above chance, that coordinate is not strong enough to carry compositional identity in this setup.

parameters.value: Blind identification accuracy above 50% for paired comparisons

dawChecklist: Create an eight-chord progression using one adjacency rule and freeze the chord labels.
Program a 60-second arrangement at 112 BPM with two-bar call and two-bar response phrases.
Duplicate the session into A, B, and C versions with identical tempo, chord labels, phrase lengths, and loudness target.
In version A, vary only voicing density, register, doublings, and chord grips.
In version B, vary only graph traversal behavior while keeping voicing style close to the control.
In version C, keep MIDI and levels fixed and vary only subtle phase/spectral processing.
Render all versions at 44.1 kHz and loudness-match them.
Blind-label paired comparisons and record whether the changed coordinate is identifiable.

protocol.listeningContext: Studio headphones plus one speaker pass at matched loudness.
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind paired comparisons between control and hidden-coordinate variants.
